routes.description: Establish God through a necessary ground of contingent existence, reinforced by the best explanation of religious experience and the objective authority of moral obligation.
routes.successCriteria: Show that at least one argument supplies a warranted bridge from the relevant experience or contingent reality to a transcendent personal ground identifiable as God.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative arguments warrant affirming that God exists.

centralBridges.description: Contingent beings require an external and ultimately necessary ground.
Mystical experience is best explained by an objective transcendent cause.
Objective moral obligation requires a transcendent ground of value.

subsidiaryBridges.description: A total explanation cannot terminate solely in unexplained contingent members.

routes.description: Defeat establishment by challenging the intelligibility and scope of metaphysical necessity and by supplying non-divine explanations or underdetermination for experiential evidence.
routes.successCriteria: Show that each offered route either relies on an unjustified conceptual extension or leaves live rival explanations that prevent the asserted inference to God.

motionBridge.description: None of the proposed routes establishes the existence of God.

centralBridges.description: Necessity and causal explanation do not validly extend to a necessary being.
Private religious reports do not discriminate God from rival mental causes.
Moral obligation and judgment admit non-divine explanatory accounts.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Observed effects and sincere reports remain compatible with false beliefs.

sections.title: Contingency and necessary existence
sections.rationale: This exchange states the principal metaphysical proof and the foundational objection to applying necessity to a being.

sections.title: Meaning of metaphysical terms
sections.rationale: The parties clarify contingency, necessity, and existence, determining whether the principal inference is even expressible.

sections.title: Explanation of the totality
sections.rationale: This section tests the decisive transition from explanations of members to an explanation outside the whole series.

sections.title: Religious experience
sections.rationale: The competing moves test whether mystical experience discriminates an objective divine cause from rival reported experiences.

sections.title: Moral obligation
sections.rationale: The final route asks whether the distinctive authority of moral obligation requires God or permits an environmental account.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Because contingent beings lack their own sufficient reason, their totality requires an external existent ground that ultimately cannot fail to exist.
moves.attributionBasis: The sustained opening presentation and explicit first-person formulation clearly identify Copleston as the speaker.

response.rationale: This is the initial constructive statement of the contingency route and therefore has no earlier selected target requiring response analysis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The opening clearly supplies premises, an intermediate regress claim, and the proposed necessary terminus.

precisionFindings.rationale: The span defines the relevant totality, external reason, regress, and being that cannot fail to exist.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is asserted as necessary although the move does not independently establish that every contingent totality needs an external reason.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The route is intelligible, but the transfer from each member's dependence to the totality's external reason remains a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Examples establish ordinary dependence, while the unrestricted sufficient-reason principle carries the decisive conclusion without separate defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central contingency bridge but does not yet identify the resulting ground as personal or good.

representationalCharity.rationale: No live opposing alternative is represented or attacked in this opening constructive move.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span contains the complete staged derivation from dependent beings through an external reason to a being that cannot not exist.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Necessity applies significantly only to analytic propositions, so a necessary being would require an existence denial that is self-contradictory.
moves.attributionBasis: The immediate turn-taking and explicit challenge to the preceding proof clearly identify Russell as the responding speaker.

components.text: Contingent beings and their totality require an external sufficient reason.
The explanatory terminus is a being whose nonexistence is impossible.

response.rationale: Russell directly attacks the necessary-being terminus by restricting necessity to analytic propositions, but he does not yet answer the sufficient-reason transition from the contingent totality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply sharply contacts one decisive component while leaving the other decisive inferential component untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: Necessity is expressly restricted to analytic propositions and self-contradictory denials, making the objection recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The semantic restriction is clearly defended, though the claim that necessity can only have this use remains contestable.

charity.alternative: Copleston proposes an actually existing being that cannot not exist as the explanatory terminus.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston reaches that being through contingent experience rather than solely through an a priori definition.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The semantic test and its consequence for necessary existence form a stable inference with one contested premise about usage.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The analytic-proposition account supplies a relevant warrant but does not establish exclusive control over all metaphysical uses of necessity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The objection directly attacks the central necessary-being bridge of the affirmative route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The necessary terminus is represented fairly, though its experiential and sufficient-reason basis is not included.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span states the semantic restriction on necessity and applies it directly to the proposed necessary being.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: A contingent being lacks the complete reason for its existence, whereas a necessary being must exist and cannot fail to exist.
moves.attributionBasis: The definitions answer Russell's immediately preceding semantic challenge and are expressly presented in Copleston's first-person terminology.

components.text: Necessity has significant application only to analytic propositions.
A necessary being requires a self-contradictory denial of existence.

response.rationale: Copleston answers the semantic challenge with operational definitions tied to explanatory dependence, preserving the legitimate question without accepting Russell's restriction to proposition types.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts both components with usable definitions, though it does not fully defend their metaphysical applicability.

precisionFindings.rationale: Both central terms receive compact and mutually consistent definitions with clear explanatory roles.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Within this move the force attaches to stipulated definitions rather than to proof that such a necessary being exists.

charity.alternative: Russell denies that necessity can significantly characterize a being rather than an analytic proposition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Russell challenges intelligibility and does not merely assert that no necessary being happens to exist.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The paired definitions are internally stable and explain how the terms differ without contradiction.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The definitions clarify usage but do not independently warrant that explanatory dependence entails the existence of the defined terminus.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the subsidiary sufficient-reason vocabulary needed by the central contingency route.

representationalCharity.rationale: It engages Russell's intelligibility objection directly, although it does not address his full analytic-proposition theory.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span supplies Copleston's explicit definitions of contingent and necessary beings and relates contingency to external explanation.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: The proposed necessary being collapses into an ontological claim, but existence is not a predicate and cannot be analytically affirmed of a named subject.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn explicitly characterizes the preceding account and continues Russell's distinctive analytic objection to necessary existence.

components.text: A contingent being lacks the complete reason for its existence.
A necessary being must exist and cannot fail to exist.

response.rationale: Russell identifies the necessary-being definition with an impermissible analytic existence claim and states the defeating consequence, while leaving the contingency definition unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply strongly contacts the decisive necessary-existence component but omits the supporting account of contingency.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection clearly distinguishes named and described subjects and explicitly denies predicate status to existence.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The logical account supports the objection, but identifying Copleston's empirical route with an ontological argument is somewhat stronger than warranted.

charity.alternative: Copleston defines a necessary being as one that must exist and cannot not exist.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston presents this definition within an argument from experienced contingency, not as a bare inference from a divine essence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The existence-not-a-predicate objection is coherent, but its application compresses the distinction between empirical and ontological routes.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A substantive logical account supports the challenge, though the asserted equivalence to Copleston's route remains insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly attacks the intelligibility of the central necessary-being conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: It captures the necessary-existence claim but omits the decisive qualification that Copleston argues from experience rather than essence alone.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span identifies the alleged ontological implication and develops the logical claim that existence cannot function as the required predicate.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: The series is either caused or uncaused; because an uncaused series would be self-sufficient and necessary despite wholly contingent members, it must have an external cause.
moves.attributionBasis: The explicit dilemma continues Copleston's first-person metaphysical case after Russell invites a ground for applying cause to the whole.

response.rationale: No earlier selected move states the immediately preceding totality objection tightly enough to serve as a valid target, so this contribution is treated as constructive.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The dilemma is explicit and advances the central route, though its exhaustive framing requires further defense.

precisionFindings.rationale: The alternatives and the claimed consequences of each are explicit, with the series consistently treated as its members' totality.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The forced choice and inference from being uncaused to being self-sufficient or necessary are asserted without excluding brute contingency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference relies on an unsupported conditional equating absence of an external cause with self-sufficiency and necessity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is conceptual and supplies no independent warrant for the decisive exhaustive dilemma or self-sufficiency step.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central contingency bridge and the proposed external-cause conclusion.

representationalCharity.rationale: No selected opposing move is represented or attacked within this constructive span.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span contains the complete caused-or-uncaused dilemma and the deductions from contingent membership to an asserted external cause.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Searching successfully for particular causes does not imply universal causation or warrant expecting the world as a whole to have an explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly answers the preceding scientific and metaphysical generalization in Russell's established negative position.

components.text: The series must be either caused or uncaused.
An uncaused series would be self-sufficient and therefore necessary.
The contingent series consequently must possess an external cause.

response.rationale: Russell diagnoses an illicit extension from successful local causal inquiry to universal and total explanation, thereby denying the warrant for both necessity and an external cause.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply contacts the decisive generalization and clearly states why the external-explanation conclusion does not follow.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between looking for particular causes and assuming causes everywhere or for the world is explicit and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move denies warranted expectation rather than claiming proof that no explanation exists, matching the supplied analogy and scope argument.

charity.alternative: Copleston argues that a contingent totality cannot be uncaused and therefore requires an external cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston's cause is transcendent rather than merely another phenomenal member of the series.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The local-to-global scope distinction directly blocks the asserted inference without creating an inconsistent contrary burden.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The search analogy and explicit scope comparison strongly support underdetermination, with a residual gap about broader sufficient reason.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the negative route's central challenge to extending causal explanation to the totality.

representationalCharity.rationale: It fairly identifies the universal explanatory expectation, though it compresses Copleston's distinction between cause and sufficient reason.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span develops the local-search analogy and expressly denies that causal inquiry entails causes everywhere or explanation of the world.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Mystical awareness of a transcendent object is not strict proof, but its basic character is best explained by an objective cause rather than a wholly subjective account.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly defines his intended category of religious experience and carefully states Copleston's explanatory conclusion.

response.rationale: This contribution opens the selected religious-experience section with a qualified constructive argument and has no earlier selected target in that section.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move defines its evidence class, limits its conclusion, and states the rival-explanation comparison clearly.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move distinguishes mystical awareness from ordinary feeling and explicitly limits the argument to best explanation rather than strict proof.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force is moderated, but the phenomenological description alone does not show that an objective divine cause is the best rival explanation.

charity.alternative: Religious experience may be explained wholly through the subject's own mental condition.
charity.decisiveQualification: The subjective alternative may explain the experience without denying its sincerity or felt certainty.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The abductive route is coherent, but the move leaves the discrimination between objective and subjective causes materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A defined experience type supplies relevant evidence, yet representative data and serious comparison with psychological alternatives are absent.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central religious-experience bridge while expressly stopping short of strict proof.

representationalCharity.rationale: The subjective alternative is acknowledged accurately, though its strongest possible mechanisms are not developed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span defines mystical experience, states its limited epistemic status, and advances an objective-cause inference against a subjective explanation.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: Equally convinced reports concern demons and other rejected entities, so recorded mystical conviction does not establish that its alleged divine object exists.
moves.attributionBasis: The explicit agnostic qualification and comparison with reports of demons identify Russell and directly answer Copleston's objective-cause inference.

components.text: Mystical experience presents itself as awareness of a transcendent object.
A wholly subjective account leaves explanatory residue.
An objective divine cause is the best explanation of the experience.

response.rationale: Russell introduces symmetrical reports with the same conviction but unacceptable objects, showing that sincerity and phenomenology do not discriminate a divine cause from error.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The symmetry objection contacts the decisive abductive bridge and makes its underdetermining consequence explicit.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is explicitly limited to what can be known from records and does not assert dogmatically that God does not exist.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The rival-report comparison warrants withholding the claimed inference while preserving Russell's expressly agnostic position.

charity.alternative: Copleston treats a narrowly defined mystical awareness as best explained by an objective transcendent cause.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston excludes ordinary visions and presents the argument as best explanation rather than strict proof.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidential symmetry between accepted and rejected reports coherently defeats inference from conviction alone.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The rival-report category is specific and relevant, though its exact phenomenological equivalence to Copleston's restricted class remains disputed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the negative route's central underdetermination challenge to religious experience.

representationalCharity.rationale: It preserves Copleston's explanatory posture but partly broadens his restricted mystical category to reports he would exclude.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span expressly preserves agnosticism while comparing mystical records with equally convinced reports about demons and devils.

moves.speaker: Frederick Copleston
moves.proposition: Widespread consciousness of moral law and obligation is best explained by a transcendent, non-arbitrary ground of value and author of the moral law.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly introduces the moral route in Copleston's first-person explanatory formulation and qualifies the proposed authorship.

response.rationale: This is the selected constructive statement of the moral-obligation route and therefore has no earlier selected target requiring response analysis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The move identifies the explanandum, proposed ground, and non-arbitrary qualification, but compresses the connecting warrant.

precisionFindings.rationale: The scope is the widespread consciousness of obligation, and the proposed transcendent author is expressly distinguished from an arbitrary legislator.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The prevalence of obligation does not by itself establish that a transcendent ground explains it better than social or psychological alternatives.

charity.alternative: Without God there may be no absolute values or absolute moral law.
charity.decisiveQualification: The converse atheist inference is treated as logical, not as an independently established premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The explanatory conclusion is intelligible, but the bridge from experienced obligation to a transcendent author remains materially undeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The prevalence claim supplies broad phenomenological support, while rival naturalistic explanations and the transcendence warrant are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly advances the central moral bridge, though it does not independently connect the ground to the stipulated personal creator.

representationalCharity.rationale: The associated atheist position is stated without caricature, although its possible qualifications are not explored.

moves.evidenceBasis: The selected span states the prevalence of moral consciousness and the inference to a transcendent, expressly non-arbitrary ground of value.

moves.speaker: Bertrand Russell
moves.proposition: The sense of moral ought can arise from imagined disapproval, customs, taboos, environment, and education rather than from a transcendent lawgiver.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly supplies Russell's environmental and psychological explanation in answer to Copleston's distinction between moral content and obligation.

components.text: Human beings widely experience a distinctive consciousness of moral obligation.
That consciousness is best explained by a transcendent ground of value.
The transcendent ground functions as a non-arbitrary author of moral law.

response.rationale: Russell accepts the phenomenon while replacing the divine explanation with psychological disapproval and socially transmitted customs, environment, and education.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The reply directly supplies a rival explanation for the decisive phenomenon, though it does not fully compare explanatory scope or normativity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move consistently addresses the experienced sense of ought and lists identifiable social and psychological explanatory sources.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The alternatives are plausible, but claiming they most easily explain moral obligation exceeds the brief associative warrant supplied.

charity.alternative: Copleston argues that moral obligation is best explained by a transcendent, non-arbitrary ground of value.
charity.decisiveQualification: Copleston distinguishes the form of obligation from culturally variable precept content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The causal alternative is coherent, but it does not fully bridge conditioned disapproval to the specifically normative appearance under dispute.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Recognizable mechanisms are supplied, yet no representative evidence establishes their adequacy for the full form of moral obligation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the negative route by offering a non-divine explanation of the moral explanandum.

representationalCharity.rationale: It engages obligation itself rather than only moral content, but does not fully preserve Copleston's form-content distinction.

moves.evidenceBasis: The span identifies imagined disapproval and socially transmitted customs, taboos, environment, and education as an alternative account of ought.
